title: Objects That Work Together: State Validation, References, Composition and Inheritance
summary: Using BankAccount, SavingsAccount and AccountBook, run code to see how names relate to objects, how methods keep the balance invariant, how composition holds other objects, and how inheritance reuses behavior; then complete withdraw, total_balance and report in the lab.

week7_review.summary: Class basics recap. The validation-free SimpleAccount shows __init__, self and instance state; LabelledAccount shows class variables and how an instance attribute shadows them; the complete classes in models.py show a shared interface. When all the assert checks at the end pass, a completion message is printed.
steps: In the Instance state line only a becomes 1200; b stays 500. In the Class variable line both objects show Campus Bank, and in the Instance shadowing line only first changes to Minsu's Bank. That is because first.bank_name = ... did not change the class variable; it created a new instance attribute on first.
Minsu's account is an object and, at the same time, an instance of BankAccount (True). A SavingsAccount object also counts as an instance of BankAccount; that is inheritance.

identity.summary: Two names can refer to one object. Assignment (alias = a) does not create a new account; it puts another name on the same object. List elements are references to objects too.
steps: Separate accounts: 1200 500 — only a received the deposit. Shared reference: 900 True — 300 was withdrawn through alias, yet a's balance dropped, and alias is a is True. Slide 8: 800 500 — accounts[0] is the same object as a (= c), so c's balance becomes 800. In the last line, even after accounts[0] is replaced with b, c is still 800. The list slot now points to a different object; the object itself did not change.
Even if the attribute values look the same, calling the class twice gives two separate objects. a is b is False, and b's balance stays 1000.
a.deposit(200) and BankAccount.deposit(a, 200) are the same call: both pass a as self. Since it ran twice, the balance becomes 1400. In real code, use only one form, once.

shared_state.summary: If a mutable list is a class attribute, every instance shares that one list. A list that each instance should have for itself is created on self in __init__.
steps: For BadBook, a name was added only to first, yet second.accounts also shows ['Minsu'], because there is only one list, on the class. IndependentBook creates a new list for each instance in __init__, so second is [].

validation.summary: The constructor rejects invalid starting values with ValueError so that an invalid account is never created, and deposit returns False for any amount that is not a positive integer, leaving the balance unchanged.
steps: The first three lines show a blank name, a negative balance and a True balance all rejected (Rejected construction). The following lines show the amount, the return value, the balance before and the balance after. 0, -10, 1.5, '10' and True are all False and the balance stays 1000; only 200 is True and gives 1200. The last two lines show why: bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance cannot filter out True, and a type(...) is int check is needed.

state_checks.summary: Run deposits and withdrawals in sequence, tracking the return value together with the balance afterward, and use assert to check both success/failure and the resulting state.
steps: The same result as the trace table on the slide: deposit 200 → True 1200, withdraw 500 → True 700, withdraw 900 → False 700 (insufficient funds), withdraw -50 → False 700 (invalid amount), withdraw 700 → True 0 (an amount equal to the balance is allowed). Rejected calls do not change the balance. All asserts pass and State checks passed is printed.

The underscore (_balance) is only a convention meaning internal use; it does not block access. Assigning to it directly from outside puts the invalid state -100 straight in. That is why the team rule to use only the public methods (deposit, withdraw, get_balance) matters.

composition.summary: AccountBook keeps references to account objects in a list (composition), and whenever it computes a total or a report it hands the work to each account's public methods (delegation).
steps: Registering the same account twice returns False the second time. After registering, withdrawing 300 from a makes book.total_balance() 700, because book did not copy the balance; it points to the same object and recalculates every time. In contrast, the report() result taken before the withdrawal (Old report values) is a list of tuples that still says 1000. A separately created empty AccountBook returns 0 and [].

inheritance.summary: SavingsAccount inherits from BankAccount, reusing its constructor validation and deposit/withdraw as they are, adds add_bonus, and overrides account_type.
steps: add_bonus is called twice: 500 + 100 + 100 = 700. add_bonus calls the inherited deposit internally, so it follows the same validation rules. The two lines below show polymorphism: the same loop prints Standard or Savings depending on the account type.

full_demo.summary: The full demo using all three classes together. This is the reference output to compare with the accounts.py you complete in Lab C.
steps: Withdraw: True 700, Rejected: False 700 (a rejected withdrawal does not change the balance), Bonus: True 600, two report lines, Total: 1300. The last line answers the checkpoint question on the slide (what is the total?).

The file name starts with a digit, so it cannot be loaded with a normal import statement; importlib was used instead. When loaded as a module, the if __name__ == "__main__": block does not run, so only the final message is printed, without the demo output.

accounts_lab.summary: Lab: complete the TODOs in BankAccount.withdraw, AccountBook.total_balance and AccountBook.report. In the starting state the first TODO raises NotImplementedError; once complete, all the checks in check_student.py should pass and the output should match 07_full_demo.
accounts_lab.notes: Edit in the terminal with nano accounts.py (save Ctrl+O, exit Ctrl+X). If you get stuck you can look at the same methods in examples/session01-v02/models.py, but the point of the lab is to write them yourself first and check with check_student.py. To submit accounts.py, run cp accounts.py /mnt/host/ and then download it from the Download box.
steps: There are three places to complete: withdraw, total_balance and report. Each TODO comment states the rules to follow.

The first withdrawal in main() raises NotImplementedError: Complete withdraw. That is expected, since it is not finished yet. Use the last line of the traceback and the line number to find which TODO it is.

The check script stops at the same place. Once the three TODOs are complete, it should end with All student checks passed. The script checks that 0, negative amounts, overdrafts, 1.5, '10' and True are all rejected, that an empty book returns 0 and [], and that the order of registration is kept.

This is the output python3 accounts.py should produce when complete (Lab C): Withdraw: True 700 … Total: 1300. Fill in the TODOs with nano accounts.py, then run python3 accounts.py and python3 check_student.py again and compare.
